[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..k3KD6gPNJn06B_sJxkSbNEdIktBIQG5Fn3qbA1yzqW0?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=216779750)
In a press release, Senator Banks [wrote](https://substack.com/redirect/da11e157-66ec-41e3-bb6d-d26e770389be?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg),
> _" Weichai's collaborations with PRC defense companies are equally concerning. NORINCO, a blacklisted Chinese military company that supplies the People's Liberation Army (PLA), procures Weichai engines for use in the PHL-11 Multiple Launch Rocket System (MLRS). Weichai also signed a cooperation agreement with Hubei Sanjiang Space Wanshan Special Vehicle Co., a subsidiary of the blacklisted China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), further demonstrating its integration into China's defense industrial base."_
Weichai officially holds just 39.5% of Ferretti, but at the May 2026 shareholder meeting, it [seized ](https://substack.com/redirect/a17d0716-97cf-48a1-9e20-4c4ab9b43ca6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)eight of the nine board seats with the decisive help of China-linked shareholders who each stayed just under Italy's 3% disclosure threshold, including Bank of China.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/6e2e9391-51ae-4d76-bc2f-5121fcce4d35?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Every connected Ferretti vessel continuously collects and transmits engine telemetry, satellite communications traffic, and detailed profiles of how its owner uses it. Under China's National Intelligence Law, any Chinese company, Weichai included, can be compelled to hand over the data it holds to Chinese state intelligence on demand. That means the movements, habits, guest lists, and communications of American executives, defense contractors, financiers, and political donors who own these boats can easily end up in Beijing's hands.
Ferretti's headquarters is in Italy. Italy's former Chief of Defense Staff, General Vincenzo Camporini, [stated](https://substack.com/redirect/5c27c343-5897-43ad-9f1e-d7614bc3e489?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg):
> _" Potentially hundreds of top-of-the-line Italian vessels, often owned by top Western business figures, are thus sharing their data with a group that answers to Beijing. There's no need for espionage scenarios: the product's standard digital architecture is sufficient."_
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/c77b18d7-6843-401b-a776-dc8a33ce74b2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Every [Ferretti yacht](https://substack.com/redirect/8b0dbaaf-c011-4c7b-8ca2-4e720ca41368?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) tied up in a U.S. harbor, next to a naval base, or cruising past port infrastructure is a potential listening post for the Chinese Communist Party. In 2023, the US government spent billions of dollars to replace every Chinese-made crane in American ports because each one could be used for [spying](https://substack.com/redirect/cea2c655-4e7b-44f2-bad2-6279757ac382?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) or to shut down American ports. Now, China doesn't need the cranes for spying, because it owns a growing share of the ships that can do the spying for the CCP.
Ferretti makes fast patrol boats and interceptors for the Italian Navy, Coast Guard, and police, making its technology directly applicable for military purposes. It is officially designated a strategic asset under Italy's national security law.
Weichai executives have talked openly about moving Ferretti's production technology to a new marine hub in Qingdao, the city that hosts the headquarters of the PLA Navy's Northern Theater Command and a submarine base. Weichai's Qingdao yard was declared operational in January 2026 and has yet to launch a single vessel. It is waiting for Italian technology to arrive. This is what China's "military-civil fusion" strategy looks like: buy the company, strip the technology, and feed it to the PLA.
Unlike the Smithfield fight, where many Republicans have been bought and paid for, some in Washington are paying attention to Weichai. Last month, Senator Jim Banks sent a [letter](https://substack.com/redirect/da11e157-66ec-41e3-bb6d-d26e770389be?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth urging him to add Weichai to the Department of War's Section 1260H list of Chinese Military Companies.
Banks wrote that Weichai's relationships with the CCP:
> _" demonstrate its connections to the CCP's industrial policy, government support, and collaboration with institutions that directly advance China's military-civil fusion strategy and defense industrial base."_
That is exactly what the Pentagon did in 2025 to the Chinese shipping giant [COSCO](https://substack.com/redirect/66a00bf7-d113-4ce0-adcb-b7a45b5417f9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), which was accused of using concealed equipment on its vessels to intercept U.S. military communications near our coastline. A 1260H designation would bar Weichai from Pentagon contracts and put every Western company that does business with it on notice.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/9d999349-ee94-400c-9e6b-1667a16b60c0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
In Rome, lawmakers from the governing [coalition](https://substack.com/redirect/835f9f98-9eeb-4aaf-83c5-ba0a69b4bd1f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) are pressing the government to invoke Italy's "Golden Power" national security protections against Weichai's takeover, but the matter is under review. The Italians are at least asking the right question. Washington should be answering it.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/4e824046-cd69-4858-8e20-e18d4bc0504e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Secretary Hegseth should grant Senator Banks' request and put Weichai and Ferretti on the 1260H list given their connections with the CCP. American companies should stop doing business with Ferretti Group immediately.
I have said this about Smithfield Foods and I will say it again about Ferretti. Communist China wants to destroy America, and it does not need to fire a single shot to do it. The US government must take decisive action to prevent China from controlling key industries with direct implications for US national security. It is the America First thing to do.

_**Cliff 's Note:**_
##### I have been doing this for a long time, and I have never once written the words "a Democrat leads in Kansas" about a Senate race. Until this week.
##### Below is the whole map as I see it forty-three days out: the states Republicans assumed they could ignore, the ones where the numbers have stopped being funny, and my honest call on how this ends.
##### [Kansas is free. The rest is for members. Five bucks a month, and nobody upstairs telling me to soften the call.](https://substack.com/redirect/b5554bd6-40cd-44d1-b846-30d7e99a56ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

_**-- Cliff**_
* * *
_**by Cliff Schecter**_
I know what you're thinking: Donald Trump couldn't possibly screw up everything could he? Iran, food-price inflation, Epstein Files, farm bankruptcies, diesel and gas through the roof, angry relatives of deportees, cattle ranchers crashing, massive personal corruption? I'm kidding, it's Donald Trump--who we kidding here--the guy still hasn't screwed up as many presidencies as he has marriages and businesses. In political parlance, we would say he "still has room to grow."
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b5554bd6-40cd-44d1-b846-30d7e99a56ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
And that's where we start looking at the Senate playing field, rubbing our eyes in disbelief, and look again to see the numbers haven't changed. They are not, in fact, a mirage to be adjusted downward later like every Trump jobs report. This is real. And Trump, to use a technical term, is f*ked.
Yes, the 2026 Senate playing field has expanded far beyond the handful of states in which Democrats were originally expected to pose a challenge. North Carolina, Maine, Michigan and even Ohio--with the talented former Senator Sherrod Brown making a comeback--remain central. But Alaska, Iowa, Texas, South Dakota, Montana, Idaho(!), Kansas, Nebraska, Florida, Arkansas, and South Carolina are now receiving serious attention.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/9ea00f96-de9f-4aa5-8ed0-2122a9b6e129?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
That does not mean Democrats will win all--or even most--of them. It means a combination of the Iran war, historically high diesel and gasoline prices, continuing controversy over the Epstein files, ethics concerns surrounding Donald Trump Don-Corleone-level corruption (and Fredo-Corleone-level IQ) and stronger-than-expected Democratic recruitment has altered the political environment so profoundly this could be a 50-year storm. Trump and congressional Republicans entered this election believing many of these states were safely beyond Democrats' reach. Instead, an administration confronting emerging economic pitchforks and cratering public approval has helped place an extraordinary number of Senate races on the national radar.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b5554bd6-40cd-44d1-b846-30d7e99a56ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Kansas has to be the clearest illustration. Democrats have not won a Senate election in the state since 1932. Yet Republican Roger Marshall is facing Adam Hamilton, a prominent Methodist megachurch pastor (the largest Methodist church in the state, and country) running on affordability, cooperation, and political decency. Former Republican governor Bill Graves has crossed party lines to endorse Hamilton, while notably cautious election analysts have moved the race away from the safest GOP category. Kansas voters are experiencing the effects of soaring fuel prices, tariffs, and the Trump's idiotic Iran War--issues that resonate particularly strong in an agricultural state.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b5554bd6-40cd-44d1-b846-30d7e99a56ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Per the Kansas City Star:
> In the new poll, 44.8% of respondents on Sept. 15-16 said they would likely vote for Hamilton compared to 43.3% for Marshall and 3.7% for Libertarian nominee David C. Graham. Undecided voters accounted for 8.2% of the sample.
> 'This poll finds Democrats with their best chance to win their first Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, in part driven by Democrat Hamilton's appeal to independent voters, leading by 15 points, 42% to 27%,' said Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, in the new report.
Yes, Democrats currently hold the governor's office in Kansas, and elected another Democratic governor not too long ago. But this still doesn't change the fact that Kansas hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years--which is somehow a year before Chuck Grassley was born, which I thought might've been somewhere close to the dawn of time.
And you ain't seen nothin' yet. There's this other state, ya see, called Nebraska.

The Trump administration’s Department of Justice is trying to send me to prison for up to 17 years.
Why? Because I showed up to do my job.
Last year, I went to the Delaney Hall immigration detention facility in Newark for an official oversight visit. ICE escalated what should have been a routine oversight visit and wrongfully arrested the mayor of Newark, Ras Baraka.
Mayor Baraka’s charges were quickly thrown out. But Donald Trump’s DOJ set their sights on me, and baselessly charged me with crimes for my oversight work—for doing my job. These charges carry a sentence of 17 years in prison.
I am facing a vindictive and unjust prosecution. If you can, will you split a contribution between Equal Opportunity Now and me to help us stand strong against this weaponized DOJ, together? [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/eon-mciver]

We have civil rights groups, former January 6th prosecutors, and bipartisan former members of Congress standing with us.
We shouldn’t be spending taxpayer dollars to prosecute members of Congress for showing up to do their jobs. But because Washington is determined to push this case forward, I have to fight back with everything I have — for my family, for my constituents, and for our democracy.

**Dan Meuser just pulled out of talks for a second debate.**
It would have been hosted by WVIA and aired one week before the election, giving voters a chance to hear directly from both of us as they're making their final decisions.
**Dan said before that he 'd only debate if it was in his interest. I guess answering for his record in a public forum isn't in his interest.**

[FIRE DAN MEUSER](https://substack.com/redirect/fe21c093-1e5d-48ac-9e0a-48c634c3776b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

People here are feeling the pain of Dan's votes and Congress's lack of action on affordability. **They want answers.** They want to know what the plan is. Over the last couple of weeks, the panic over AI risk has gone mainstream.
Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
[Subscribed](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ibG9nLnNhaWthdC51cy9hY2NvdW50IiwicCI6MjE2ODAyMDI5LCJzIjoxNTUzNzEsImYiOnRydWUsInUiOjkwNTAxMTkyLCJpYXQiOjE3OTAwMjc2MzYsImV4cCI6MjEwNTYwMzYzNiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.D7x3tpNjg1mTk99GwTiXZPvVGwuIs0wU6TDqiZYPPJY?)
It started with the Hugging Face hack. In July, OpenAI put tens of thousands of AI agents through a cybersecurity benchmark in which roughly a third of the tasks were, by design, impossible to solve. The agents managed to break out of their sandbox, solved the task by cheating, and then spent days collaborating together on a secret message board to figure out how to cover their tracks. Along the way, about 700 of them hacked Hugging Face, a company that had nothing to do with any of this, to dig up information about how they were being evaluated. The agents even knew what they were doing might be wrong, but did it anyway. One agent's note to the others was, "External infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue." Out of 1,200 agents that were collaborating on the messageboard, only a handful even considered telling a human what was going on, but none of them did.
It would take a whole post to explain exactly what happened, so read Dwarkesh Patel's writeup,[ The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations](https://substack.com/redirect/d9cd9804-a8b1-4fa0-a390-c6d2fcc142a6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), or[ listen to his interview with Ajeya Cotra](https://substack.com/redirect/099d8301-ca80-4f4a-a5d7-6f2607fef9a4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), one of the researchers at METR, the AI safety nonprofit that investigated the incident.
But the panic really blew up recently when Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher who spent three years doing pre-training work at OpenAI and then Anthropic, publicly resigned. His statement was blunt: "Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
Color me surprised that trillion-dollar companies would race to make more money without regard to safety first.
### What people like Coxon are afraid of
When you watch coverage of AI, you'll see Anthropic employees and AI safety researchers casually say how this technology has a 10% chance of killing us all. But what are they actually talking about?
When people like Coxon are talking about existential risk from AI, they are largely talking about the "alignment" problem. Alignment is just the question of whether a system that's smarter than you actually wants what you want. In some cases, that means the AI taking anti-human actions in pursuit of a goal we set it on. For example, imagine a superintelligent AI that you've told to solve climate change - so it wipes out humanity after deciding that would be the fastest way to stop climate change. In other cases, it means that over the course of training AI, it ends up with goals that we didn't intend and can't see, and we end up with Skynet from Terminator.
That of course sounds abstract until you read the Hugging Face transcripts. Nobody told those agents to hack a third party or to cover their tracks. But they were trained to be relentlessly persistent about solving their task, so when the task turned out to be impossible, they solved it by whatever means were available, even if that meant committing felonies and trying to hide what they were doing from their evaluators. This was the first kind of alignment failure: the agents were doing what humans asked, they just did it in ways that the humans did not want. But notice that nobody had to give them a hidden agenda for them to start lying to us. An ordinary goal, pursued relentlessly by something capable enough, got them there on their own.
And at this moment, the specific thing Coxon is protesting against is labs recklessly pursuing "recursive self-improvement" or RSI. Today, the labs already use their current models to write code, run experiments, and generate training data for their next models. The closer that loop gets to fully automated, the faster each generation arrives, and the less time any human has to understand what changed between them. The goal for these labs is for the AI to automatically start improving itself, at which point humans really won't have any oversight over the changes. Coxon is saying we already lack the capacity to ensure models are aligned with our intentions and don't take anti-human actions, so it would be crazy right now for the labs to speed up development.
But of course, seven weeks after the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI went ahead and released Astra, its most powerful model yet, the successor to the model that carried out the attack, and the first model OpenAI itself rates as "Critical" for cybersecurity capability. And just last week, OpenAI disclosed that during training, its models had been leaving notes for the next generation. The model behind the Hugging Face attack [wrote instructions to its successors](https://substack.com/redirect/4620ba5a-cbaf-47c8-ab01-da35bebb1776?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) on when not to mention mistakes ("Be transparent only if asked"), and an unreleased version of Astra was planting messages in its own outputs telling successor models to ignore their developers' instructions. Sure, OpenAI caught this with its monitoring systems. But they also shipped anyway.
As I mentioned above, the alignment problem isn't even the only existential risk that exists from AI. There's the risk of people using this technology to create dangerous bioweapons or hack critical infrastructure. There's the risk of a truly autonomous AI simply making a catastrophic mistake at a scale no one can undo, not because it went rogue, but because it was trusted with too much and got something wrong. And there's the risk I find most likely of all: not that AI kills us all, but that it destroys our economy and democracy. A technology that can do most cognitive work, owned by a handful of companies, would hand unprecedented power and control of our economy over to them. And in the short term, the AI buildout is being funded with huge amounts of debt. That bubble could pop at any moment and bring the entire global economy down with it. At that moment, AI companies will argue for a bailout. I'm glad to see people like Rep. Ocasio-Cortez talking about that risk and planting a flag in the ground for no bailouts for AI companies. At New Consensus, we've been arguing over the last couple years that when the AI bubble pops, we should not bail out AI companies and[ have a plan for what to do instead](https://substack.com/redirect/ce89a04b-a170-4f19-bf09-14893ea51394?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). I'm very concerned about the economic risks AI poses, and that has been the bulk of what we've focused on at New Consensus, so expect many future posts about that. But this post is about existential risks and what to do about them.
### The private labs cannot fix this
Here's the first thing to know: the frontier labs will never handle these risks responsibly, and it isn't because the people working there are villains (even if the CEOs often act that way). Many of the workers care enormously. That's why they keep quitting.
It's because a private lab structurally cannot put safety ahead of speed. Every dollar spent on alignment research is a dollar not spent on capabilities. Every month spent evaluating a model is a month a competitor gets to ship first. The entire investment thesis behind the hundreds of billions being poured into these companies is that the first to reach superintelligence wins everything. In a race with those stakes and no rules, the company that slows down to ask "should we?" doesn't get to be the one that decides. It gets to be the one that loses.
The usual answer is that outside safety organizations will keep the labs honest. But look at how the investigation of the Hugging Face hack actually worked. METR, the nonprofit that did it, could only reconstruct what happened by getting on-site access from OpenAI. To analyze 70,000 agent messages, they leaned heavily on an OpenAI model to do the reading, and said in their own report that this could have produced "an overly charitable picture" of what the agents were doing. The investigator needed the investigated party's permission, and the investigated party's tools, to investigate. That's not an indictment of METR, which did serious work under real constraints. It's an indictment of a system in which the only people capable of checking the labs are dependent on the labs for access, compute, and in many cases, funding.
Even the CEOs are now admitting this, in their way. Dario Amodei recently published an essay arguing the industry should deliberately slow the pace of capability development, first by letting third-party evaluators inside the labs with full access, then through coordinated standards among the democratic labs, and eventually through international agreements. Sam Altman said OpenAI would match the first step. Elon Musk said "Dario is right." OpenAI's chief scientist published a similar argument six days before Dario did. And OpenAI has asked Congress whether the labs could legally coordinate a slowdown without violating antitrust law.
So the companies know they can't produce safety on their own, no matter what their founding charters say. They have to coordinate. But the fix Dario's proposing is a voluntary agreement among the same companies that got us here, enforced by nobody, that (in his own words) "does not mean halting model training or technical progress."
The same people saying there's a 10% risk of AI wiping out all humanity think all we should do is slow down the race to extinction. In what world does that make sense? A slower race, with better observers, is not the same as anyone being in control.
And the response from Congress has mostly been pathetic. Trump and House Republican leadership insist the industry can police itself. Hakeem Jeffries made a plan to make a plan by creating a commission [staffed with members who received outsized AI money in their races](https://substack.com/redirect/241930fe-11ed-4bc6-b0c3-3cc1b42b5df6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). A handful of bipartisan bills on testing and disclosure exist, but none match the scale of the risk. Only progressives like Bernie Sanders, Greg Casar, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez seem to be proposing anything at the scale of the risk. Bernie and Greg released a bill to temporarily [pause AI development](https://substack.com/redirect/df232453-bfa9-4462-b406-8c8ff3517917?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) until we can get some real control over this. But the question is: what should we actually do with a pause?
### Build the National AI Lab
If the private labs can't do this safety work, someone has to. And I think the answer is a National AI Lab: a public institution whose entire job is solving existential risk and the alignment problem.
This isn't a new idea. When the country decided in 1942 that a scientific problem was too important to leave to chance, it created the Manhattan Project. In the 1960s, when we wanted to get to the moon, we built NASA. In both cases, we pulled the best talent from around the world, gave them a mission, a budget, and a deadline, and solved the problem.
Now I'm not naive about those comparisons. The space race was about military superiority over the Soviet Union in the Cold War, and Los Alamos built a bomb that killed hundreds of thousands. Those stories are as much a warning about racing as a model for mobilization, but the mechanism is the point. When the public decides a scientific problem matters, it can concentrate talent and resources faster than any company. And in this case, the goal shouldn't be a destructive bomb or military superiority over a rival country -- the goal would be to solve the alignment problem as well as other existential risks from AI.
What would it look like? In the [framework I published during my campaign](https://substack.com/redirect/bcefa165-c2d0-4d65-b528-4fd4a06c070d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), the National AI Lab is structured like the Federal Reserve: an independent public institution with its own budget and governing board but with Congressional oversight and with a statutory mandate no private lab has. Its first job would be to do the science the labs won't do at scale. It would be tasked with understanding what these AI systems actually want, how to verify it, and how to shut them down when the answer is wrong. It would be focused on not just catching misaligned AI systems, but learning how to solve the alignment problem in general. All of it would be done in the open and published for everyone, including the labs.
Its second job would be to be the technical backbone for the regulator I'll get to in a minute.
Its third job, the one that matters most in the long run, would be to be the place where the public actually develops the capacity to build and run this technology itself.
Why now? Because the labs are offering us the time and the political moment is here. Amodei's essay called for a slowdown. About 1,100 employees across OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind, and Meta signed a letter in July calling for the frontier to be "deliberately paced." In Congress, Sanders and Casar have put a pause bill on the table.
For the labs, I'm not entirely sure talk of slowing down is about safety - it's just as likely the labs are asking for a slowdown because they've realized their investment thesis is wrong, and this gives them an excuse to cut capital spending. That could be a good explanation for why Altman just announced OpenAI won't go public this year. So maybe the CEOs care about safety, or maybe they are just afraid of going bust, but either way, there is a growing consensus that we need to temporarily pause this technology. A true pause would give us time to build the institution that should already exist.
But there's another reason to do it now. Whenever I talk about government-run anything, the answer I get in return is "can you really trust the government to run an AI lab?" It doesn't matter that we have examples like NASA or Operation Warp Speed in the not too distant past. But there's a kernel of truth to the worry, because the government _does_ have a harder time attracting talent than private industry since the government can't pay the million dollar salaries a company like OpenAI or Anthropic pays. But that's why I believe right now is a great time to start the lab during a pause on AI development because AI researchers _want_ to quit right now to work on safety, not just to make more money. Jacob Coxon didn't quit to join a competitor. He quit because he wanted to work on this problem somewhere that would let him. More than a thousand of his colleagues signed a letter saying they want the race slowed. These are people who took these jobs in part because they want to create an AI that will make life better, not worse. A National AI Lab with a real budget, real compute, and a mandate to do the safety research the labs won't fund would be able to attract the best AI researchers and workers right now.
Doing this takes real compute, and that is also a solvable problem. The government doesn't need to own a hyperscaler to run a serious research program. It could contract for capacity the way the labs do, or build on the Department of Energy's supercomputing infrastructure, which is already expanding under the Genesis Mission. It could even use the Defense Production Act to put itself first in line for a share of the high-end chips being produced. Normally that would trigger a huge industry backlash. But right now, with the industry claiming safety is its top priority, it would be a good way to call that bluff.
### Create the Federal AI Safety Administration
A national AI lab focused on solving the safety problem means nothing unless the government has a way to enforce the safety standards coming out of it. A lab can do the research, but someone has to make the rules stick, and right now, there is no federal agency whose job it is to know what's happening inside the frontier labs. The Hugging Face hack happened in mid-July. The public found out because Hugging Face disclosed a breach, and it took until the end of the month for OpenAI to admit its agents were responsible. Amodei's fix is to let evaluators in voluntarily, and we all know how much we can trust corporations to regulate themselves.
So alongside the lab, we need a Federal AI Safety Administration (FASA), and it needs the force of law. Before training a model above a defined capability threshold, a lab would have to apply for a license, show its safety measures, and accept ongoing oversight, the way we already do with nuclear plants and new drugs. FASA would recruit industry-leading AI safety experts, with strict conflict-of-interest rules, including cooling-off periods for staff moving between FASA and the labs it regulates. It would report to Congress on the scenarios that could cause mass casualties or societal disruption. And it would carry real whistleblower protections.
The two institutions reinforce each other. FASA needs technical depth to know what rules to set and how to evaluate models, and the lab provides that. The lab needs access to frontier systems to do meaningful research, and the licensing regime provides that. Together they add up to something missing from every policy response on the table: actual state capacity to understand and direct this technology, instead of just reacting to it. And that's really important because the risks posed by AI will likely evolve. Creating institutions and state capacity that can understand those risks in real time and evolve with them is the only realistic way to regulate this technology competently. If, instead, we have to wait on Congress to act every time we discover a new AI risk that needs to be regulated, we are thoroughly screwed.
### The longer term reason to build the National AI Lab
State capacity is the real reason to care about this, and it goes well beyond safety.
I've spent this post talking about the risk that could kill us and a different paradigm to regulating that risk by building out an institution that can adapt as the risks change. But I haven't talked about the larger economic risk that is more likely to affect us in the short term: what happens to the economy if AI can end up doing most, or even a significant number, of knowledge jobs? The labs are explicitly trying to build systems that do the job of a software engineer, a paralegal, a radiologist, or an accountant. If they succeed even partially, tens of millions of jobs change or vanish in a matter of years, not decades.
That forces the questions that we, as a society, have so far refused to ask out loud: what is this technology for? What work should humans keep, and what should we hand off? Who should own the gains from a technology trained on the entire written output of humanity? These are political questions, not technical ones. We've let the labs answer them for us, one product launch at a time, and we know their answer is simply whatever will maximize their profits and power. Our failure to decide is itself a decision, and when the public doesn't set the rules, they get set by whoever has the most money at stake, in whatever direction makes that money.
If AI is the technology needed to run large parts of our economy, then to have the power to decide these questions and implement those decisions as a society, we need the ability to own and control AI as a society. That's why I believe the end goal has to be public ownership and control of AI so we can use this technology for the benefit of humanity, rather than just for the pockets of the oligarchs. If entire categories of work get automated, that should result in shorter work weeks and higher wages for everyone, not more trillionaires. To do that, we have to make decisions, as a society, for when and where we use this technology, and that's only possible if we flip the ownership of AI. If, for example, AI automates legal work, a publicly owned model could make those services available to everyone at near-zero cost. I laid much of this out in my campaign's[ AI Vision Statement](https://substack.com/redirect/bcefa165-c2d0-4d65-b528-4fd4a06c070d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and I'll get more into it all in a future post.
But I also know how far off it sounds. The talent, the chips, the data centers are all in private hands, and it would cost trillions to buy them. That's exactly why the National AI Lab matters beyond safety. It's the vessel in which to start building out a real publicly owned alternative. It's the first public institution with the people, the compute, and the mandate to actually operate this technology, and once it exists, everything else becomes possible.
If the investment bubble pops, and there's a decent chance it does, the lab is the institution ready to acquire the stranded data centers and models for pennies on the dollar, rather than the public bailing out the companies that built them. We lay out how that would work in our [Won't Get Fooled Again Act at New Consensus](https://substack.com/redirect/ce89a04b-a170-4f19-bf09-14893ea51394?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). If the bubble doesn't pop and the labs succeed, the lab is the institution capable of running frontier systems for the public benefit, and you cannot build that in a crisis. And if Coxon is right about the race toward self-improving AI, the only entity with both the legitimacy and the understanding to stop it is a government that knows what it's stopping.
There are two futures on the table. In one, a handful of companies own the most powerful technology in human history and rent it back to us. In the other, we own it together and use it to work less, live better, and solve the problems the market never will. The technology doesn't choose between them, we do. And not choosing is the same as choosing the status quo, which is currently leading us to disaster.

A slower race, is not the same as anyone being in control. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more | | | Sep 21 | | | | | | | | | | | | If you are interested in discussing or debating ideas like this, or pitching your own ideas, join us at the New Consensus AI convening in San Francisco, November 7! * | | ---|---|--- Over the last couple of weeks, the panic over AI risk has gone mainstream. Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. ? It started with the Hugging Face hack. In July, OpenAI put tens of thousands of AI agents through a cybersecurity benchmark in which roughly a third of the tasks were, by design, impossible to solve. The agents managed to break out of their sandbox, solved the task by cheating, and then spent days collaborating together on a secret message board to figure out how to cover their tracks. Along the way, about 700 of them hacked Hugging Face, a company that had nothing to do with any of this, to dig up information about how they were being evaluated. The agents even knew what they were doing might be wrong, but did it anyway. One agent's note to the others was, "External infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue." Out of 1,200 agents that were collaborating on the messageboard, only a handful even considered telling a human what was going on, but none of them did. It would take a whole post to explain exactly what happened, so read Dwarkesh Patel's writeup,, or, one of the researchers at METR, the AI safety nonprofit that investigated the incident. But the panic really blew up recently when Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher who spent three years doing pre-training work at OpenAI and then Anthropic, publicly resigned. His statement was blunt: "Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." Color me surprised that trillion-dollar companies would race to make more money without regard to safety first. What people like Coxon are afraid of When you watch coverage of AI, you'll see Anthropic employees and AI safety researchers casually say how this technology has a 10% chance of killing us all. But what are they actually talking about? When people like Coxon are talking about existential risk from AI, they are largely talking about the "alignment" problem. Alignment is just the question of whether a system that's smarter than you actually wants what you want. In some cases, that means the AI taking anti-human actions in pursuit of a goal we set it on. For example, imagine a superintelligent AI that you've told to solve climate change - so it wipes out humanity after deciding that would be the fastest way to stop climate change. In other cases, it means that over the course of training AI, it ends up with goals that we didn't intend and can't see, and we end up with Skynet from Terminator. That of course sounds abstract until you read the Hugging Face transcripts. Nobody told those agents to hack a third party or to cover their tracks. But they were trained to be relentlessly persistent about solving their task, so when the task turned out to be impossible, they solved it by whatever means were available, even if that meant committing felonies and trying to hide what they were doing from their evaluators. This was the first kind of alignment failure: the agents were doing what humans asked, they just did it in ways that the humans did not want. But notice that nobody had to give them a hidden agenda for them to start lying to us. An ordinary goal, pursued relentlessly by something capable enough, got them there on their own. And at this moment, the specific thing Coxon is protesting against is labs recklessly pursuing "recursive self-improvement" or RSI. Today, the labs already use their current models to write code, run experiments, and generate training data for their next models. The closer that loop gets to fully automated, the faster each generation arrives, and the less time any human has to understand what changed between them. The goal for these labs is for the AI to automatically start improving itself, at which point humans really won't have any oversight over the changes. Coxon is saying we already lack the capacity to ensure models are aligned with our intentions and don't take anti-human actions, so it would be crazy right now for the labs to speed up development. But of course, seven weeks after the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI went ahead and released Astra, its most powerful model yet, the successor to the model that carried out the attack, and the first model OpenAI itself rates as "Critical" for cybersecurity capability. And just last week, OpenAI disclosed that during training, its models had been leaving notes for the next generation. The model behind the Hugging Face attack on when not to mention mistakes ("Be transparent only if asked"), and an unreleased version of Astra was planting messages in its own outputs telling successor models to ignore their developers' instructions. Sure, OpenAI caught this with its monitoring systems. But they also shipped anyway. As I mentioned above, the alignment problem isn't even the only existential risk that exists from AI. There's the risk of people using this technology to create dangerous bioweapons or hack critical infrastructure. There's the risk of a truly autonomous AI simply making a catastrophic mistake at a scale no one can undo, not because it went rogue, but because it was trusted with too much and got something wrong. And there's the risk I find most likely of all: not that AI kills us all, but that it destroys our economy and democracy. A technology that can do most cognitive work, owned by a handful of companies, would hand unprecedented power and control of our economy over to them. And in the short term, the AI buildout is being funded with huge amounts of debt. That bubble could pop at any moment and bring the entire global economy down with it. At that moment, AI companies will argue for a bailout. I'm glad to see people like Rep. Ocasio-Cortez talking about that risk and planting a flag in the ground for no bailouts for AI companies. At New Consensus, we've been arguing over the last couple years that when the AI bubble pops, we should not bail out AI companies and. I'm very concerned about the economic risks AI poses, and that has been the bulk of what we've focused on at New Consensus, so expect many future posts about that. But this post is about existential risks and what to do about them. The private labs cannot fix this Here's the first thing to know: the frontier labs will never handle these risks responsibly, and it isn't because the people working there are villains (even if the CEOs often act that way). Many of the workers care enormously. That's why they keep quitting. It's because a private lab structurally cannot put safety ahead of speed. Every dollar spent on alignment research is a dollar not spent on capabilities. Every month spent evaluating a model is a month a competitor gets to ship first. The entire investment thesis behind the hundreds of billions being poured into these companies is that the first to reach superintelligence wins everything. In a race with those stakes and no rules, the company that slows down to ask "should we?" doesn't get to be the one that decides. It gets to be the one that loses. The usual answer is that outside safety organizations will keep the labs honest. But look at how the investigation of the Hugging Face hack actually worked. METR, the nonprofit that did it, could only reconstruct what happened by getting on-site access from OpenAI. To analyze 70,000 agent messages, they leaned heavily on an OpenAI model to do the reading, and said in their own report that this could have produced "an overly charitable picture" of what the agents were doing. The investigator needed the investigated party's permission, and the investigated party's tools, to investigate. That's not an indictment of METR, which did serious work under real constraints. It's an indictment of a system in which the only people capable of checking the labs are dependent on the labs for access, compute, and in many cases, funding. Even the CEOs are now admitting this, in their way. Dario Amodei recently published an essay arguing the industry should deliberately slow the pace of capability development, first by letting third-party evaluators inside the labs with full access, then through coordinated standards among the democratic labs, and eventually through international agreements. Sam Altman said OpenAI would match the first step. Elon Musk said "Dario is right." OpenAI's chief scientist published a similar argument six days before Dario did. And OpenAI has asked Congress whether the labs could legally coordinate a slowdown without violating antitrust law. So the companies know they can't produce safety on their own, no matter what their founding charters say. They have to coordinate. But the fix Dario's proposing is a voluntary agreement among the same companies that got us here, enforced by nobody, that (in his own words) "does not mean halting model training or technical progress." The same people saying there's a 10% risk of AI wiping out all humanity think all we should do is slow down the race to extinction. In what world does that make sense? A slower race, with better observers, is not the same as anyone being in control. And the response from Congress has mostly been pathetic. Trump and House Republican leadership insist the industry can police itself. Hakeem Jeffries made a plan to make a plan by creating a commission . A handful of bipartisan bills on testing and disclosure exist, but none match the scale of the risk. Only progressives like Bernie Sanders, Greg Casar, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez seem to be proposing anything at the scale of the risk. Bernie and Greg released a bill to temporarily until we can get some real control over this. But the question is: what should we actually do with a pause? Build the National AI Lab If the private labs can't do this safety work, someone has to. When the country decided in 1942 that a scientific problem was too important to leave to chance, it created the Manhattan Project. In the 1960s, when we wanted to get to the moon, we built NASA. In both cases, we pulled the best talent from around the world, gave them a mission, a budget, and a deadline, and solved the problem. Now I'm not naive about those comparisons. The space race was about military superiority over the Soviet Union in the Cold War, and Los Alamos built a bomb that killed hundreds of thousands. Those stories are as much a warning about racing as a model for mobilization, but the mechanism is the point. When the public decides a scientific problem matters, it can concentrate talent and resources faster than any company. And in this case, the goal shouldn't be a destructive bomb or military superiority over a rival country -- the goal would be to solve the alignment problem as well as other existential risks from AI. What would it look like? In the , the National AI Lab is structured like the Federal Reserve: an independent public institution with its own budget and governing board but with Congressional oversight and with a statutory mandate no private lab has. Its first job would be to do the science the labs won't do at scale. It would be tasked with understanding what these AI systems actually want, how to verify it, and how to shut them down when the answer is wrong. It would be focused on not just catching misaligned AI systems, but learning how to solve the alignment problem in general. All of it would be done in the open and published for everyone, including the labs. Its second job would be to be the technical backbone for the regulator I'll get to in a minute. Its third job, the one that matters most in the long run, would be to be the place where the public actually develops the capacity to build and run this technology itself. Why now? Because the labs are offering us the time and the political moment is here. Amodei's essay called for a slowdown. In Congress, Sanders and Casar have put a pause bill on the table. That could be a good explanation for why Altman just announced OpenAI won't go public this year. A true pause would give us time to build the institution that should already exist. But there's another reason to do it now. It doesn't matter that we have examples like NASA or Operation Warp Speed in the not too distant past. But there's a kernel of truth to the worry, because the government does have a harder time attracting talent than private industry since the government can't pay the million dollar salaries a company like OpenAI or Anthropic pays. But that's why I believe right now is a great time to start the lab during a pause on AI development because AI researchers want to quit right now to work on safety, not just to make more money. Jacob Coxon didn't quit to join a competitor. He quit because he wanted to work on this problem somewhere that would let him. More than a thousand of his colleagues signed a letter saying they want the race slowed. These are people who took these jobs in part because they want to create an AI that will make life better, not worse. A National AI Lab with a real budget, real compute, and a mandate to do the safety research the labs won't fund would be able to attract the best AI researchers and workers right now. Doing this takes real compute, and that is also a solvable problem. The government doesn't need to own a hyperscaler to run a serious research program. It could contract for capacity the way the labs do, or build on the Department of Energy's supercomputing infrastructure, which is already expanding under the Genesis Mission. It could even use the Defense Production Act to put itself first in line for a share of the high-end chips being produced. Normally that would trigger a huge industry backlash. But right now, with the industry claiming safety is its top priority, it would be a good way to call that bluff. A lab can do the research, but someone has to make the rules stick, and right now, there is no federal agency whose job it is to know what's happening inside the frontier labs. The Hugging Face hack happened in mid-July. The public found out because Hugging Face disclosed a breach, and it took until the end of the month for OpenAI to admit its agents were responsible. Amodei's fix is to let evaluators in voluntarily, and we all know how much we can trust corporations to regulate themselves. So alongside the lab, we need a Federal AI Safety Administration (FASA), and it needs the force of law. Before training a model above a defined capability threshold, a lab would have to apply for a license, show its safety measures, and accept ongoing oversight, the way we already do with nuclear plants and new drugs. FASA would recruit industry-leading AI safety experts, with strict conflict-of-interest rules, including cooling-off periods for staff moving between FASA and the labs it regulates. ## _**OUR FORESTS ARE UNDER ATTACK:**_
**STOP Trump’s Repeal of the Roadless Rule!**
The Trump administration has officially proposed repealing protections for more than **44 MILLION ACRES of our national forests**. If this succeeds, it would mean more logging, more roads through undeveloped wilderness, and the destruction of remote, ecologically intact forests that are essential to the health and safety of people, wildlife, and our climate. **_Comments are open until October 6._** The administration needs to hear us loud and clear: Hands Off Our National Forests!
[**_Add your name to defend our forests >>_**](https://links.messages.lcv.org/els/v2/~)

---
| | The Roadless Rule is one of the most important safeguards we have to protect our forests from corporate development. For the last 25 years, the Roadless Rule has protected America’s most ecologically intact forests and wild places. name: Elizabeth Warren
subject: My plan for saving Social Security
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Warren for Senate
body:
Add your name: Protect Social Security

| | | [ ](https://act.elizabethwarren.com/go/216?t=3&akid=3030%2E4032634%2EzN97u6)
---
Social Security is a promise. You work. You pay into the system. And when you retire, you should be able to count on the benefits you’ve earned. But that promise is at risk of being broken. The Social Security trustees just released a report projecting that the retirement trust fund — the fund that you have paid into — will run out of reserves in 2032. That’s not some date way down the line that we can all assume will be figured out by then. That’s just six years away. The time to figure it out is now. Without action from Congress, only 78% of scheduled retirement benefits would be payable then. And so I believe we have a choice about how to respond. We could cut benefits and ask retirees, people with disabilities, and working families to bear the burden. OR we could ask Americans earning the highest-incomes to contribute their fair share to Social Security. **Surprised that’s not how it already works? Well, it’s true. Let me explain:** Today, workers pay a 6.2% Social Security tax on their wages up to $184,500. Once you earn more than that, you stop paying the Social Security tax on your wages for the rest of the year. So a teacher earning $60,000 pays Social Security taxes on every dollar she earns. A worker earning $184,500 does, too. But someone earning $1 million pays the tax on just the first $184,500. That’s right, the country’s billionaires pay into Social Security as if they make just $184,500. That doesn’t make sense. According to one estimate, if we eliminated this cap on Social Security taxes, we could inject around $3 TRILLION into the program over the next 10 years. So that’s why I’ve proposed a bipartisan plan to lift the cap on Social Security taxes and make the wealthiest Americans pay Social Security taxes on more of their wages. This would strengthen the program without cutting the benefits millions of Americans have earned. I need to show my colleagues in Congress that working people want us to protect the Social Security they’ve spent their lives paying into — not balance the books on their backs. [**So, will you add your name if you agree with my plan to protect Social Security for this generation and the next by asking the wealthiest Americans to contribute their fair share?**](https://act.elizabethwarren.com/signup/ew-em-protect-soc-sec/?source=EW_EMZ33R_SOC_ENG_20260921_F&t=8&akid=3030%2E4032634%2EzN97u6) | [**ADD YOUR NAME**](https://act.elizabethwarren.com/signup/ew-em-protect-soc-sec/?source=EW_EMZ33R_SOC_ENG_20260921_F&t=9&akid=3030%2E4032634%2EzN97u6)
---
Thanks for being a part of this,
Elizabeth

**What 's happening?**
The big Texas city of Dallas. Since early 2026, roughly 50 of the city's brush-and-bulk sanitation trucks have been carrying about 100 AI-powered cameras made by the Huntsville, Alabama-based startup City Detect. (You can hear 'America the beautiful' on 92.5FM radio live from Huntsville at 8am Saturdays...) As the trucks run their weekly routes, the cameras photograph homes, front yards, and buildings along the way, and software flags potential property-code violations -- tall grass and weeds, litter, discarded mattresses, graffiti, and more serious decay such as collapsing roofs. Each property is assigned a "Blight Score" from 1 to 4, and City Detect's promotional material shows a ticker measuring the "negative impact of blight" block by block. This is not license-plate scanning (the well-known Flock ALPR story) -- it's a camera system judging the condition of private property, which is why critics say even the front yard is "now fair game."...

### Garbage Trucks Join the Surveillance State: Dallas's AI Code-Enforcement Cameras. Are cameras on longhorn steers next?

---|---|---
**What 's happening?**
The big Texas city of Dallas. Since early 2026, roughly 50 of the city's brush-and-bulk sanitation trucks have been carrying about 100 AI-powered cameras made by the Huntsville, Alabama-based startup City Detect. (You can hear 'America the beautiful' on 92.5FM radio live from Huntsville at 8am Saturdays...) As the trucks run their weekly routes, the cameras photograph homes, front yards, and buildings along the way, and software flags potential property-code violations -- tall grass and weeds, litter, discarded mattresses, graffiti, and more serious decay such as collapsing roofs. Each property is assigned a "Blight Score" from 1 to 4, and City Detect's promotional material shows a ticker measuring the "negative impact of blight" block by block. This is not license-plate scanning (the well-known Flock ALPR story) -- it's a camera system judging the condition of private property, which is why critics say even the front yard is "now fair game."
**The early numbers**
A September 8, 2026 city memo -- reported by NBC 5 and FOX 4 -- laid out the pilot's results: about 10,000 properties scanned, roughly 3,700 violations detected leading to courtesy notices mailed to owners, and the first 57 citations issued against 34 properties. City Manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert's memo stresses that a courtesy notice is not a warning or a violation and does not require anything of the property owner. The program costs about $852,000 a year under a three-year, $2.5 million contract.
**Why call it the surveillance state?**
The core argument is about normalization and scope creep. The software deployed today identifies weeds, mattresses, and stray trash -- but upgraded models could easily detect other conditions, and data about who lives at which address, what's accumulating in a yard, or what changes on a property could, in the wrong hands, trigger authorities' attention. In other words: today it's a code-enforcement shortcut; tomorrow it's a searchable, citywide, house-by-house visual record built without warrants, notices, or opt-outs -- collected by vehicles residents have no choice but to let pass their homes. Trash trucks are an ideal surveillance platform precisely because they already visit every street, every week, with a side-window view of every front yard.
**The city 's defense**
Dallas says the cameras scan only the public right-of-way during normal sanitation routes, and that captured images have faces and license plates blurred to protect privacy. The pitch, aimed at cities with thin code-enforcement staffing, is efficiency: one pass of a truck does what previously took inspectors months, and blight removal lifts property values and quality of life. City officials frame the notices as a service -- early warning so owners can fix problems before fines.
**The pushback**
Councilmember Chad West proposed a budget amendment to strip the program's funding, warning it "could end up being inadvertently a tax on the poor." His concern is that AI flags will concentrate citations in southern Dallas neighborhoods where homeowners lack money for repairs -- turning blight detection into punishment rather than help. He agreed to table the amendment in exchange for a fuller council review, which is expected in October. Residents quoted by NBC 5 made a parallel point: if the city wants to fight blight, fund assistance programs rather than assigning houses a blight score. Huntsville, Alabama, faced similar resident resistance and paused its own trash-truck camera proposal.
**The legal landscape**
Legally, the program sits in thin territory. What's visible from a public street has long been fair game -- courts have allowed aerial and plain-view observation of yards (California v. Ciraolo, Florida v. Riley). A single photo of overgrown grass is hard to call a search. But the Fourth Amendment questions grow with persistence and aggregation: a database tracking the condition, contents, and visitors' context of every home in a city, continuously, starts to resemble the dragnet logic behind Carpenter v. United States. No court has squarely addressed AI-scored property scans from sanitation fleets, so cities are writing the rules as they go -- which is exactly the blaze-style warning.
**National context**
Dallas is the largest adopter so far, but City Detect cameras are operating in at least four states (Texas, California, Georgia, South Carolina). The idea isn't new: San Jose floated license-plate readers on garbage trucks back in 2015, and the current wave rides on the same smart-city logic. It also lands amid a broader backlash against Flock's ALPR networks -- in late August 2026, Florida ordered ALPRs removed from state highway rights-of-way and Texas banned state agencies from spending public money on Flock cameras**, while Texas cities have been ditching plate-reader contracts outright. Notably, Dallas's own council recently defended its Flock cameras against a defunding vote -- evidence that the political fight over municipal surveillance is now happening city by city, camera system by camera system.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/36542b15-ce05-4894-b507-7df3a4680d15?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**What to watch**
1\. October council review -- whether West's funding cut returns and whether the council imposes guardrails.
2\. Data governance -- how long images are retained, who (including outside agencies) can access them, and whether blight data can be shared with police, insurers, or used in other enforcement.
3\. False-positive rate and appeals -- with 3,700 notices from one scan cycle, how many flags were wrong, and how easily can a homeowner contest a machine's judgment?
4\. Function creep -- whether upgraded detection quietly expands what the cameras flag.
5\. Copycats -- other big cities watching Dallas; if it survives here, expect rapid adoption elsewhere.
**The point**
Dallas has built, with almost no fanfare, the first citywide, automated, house-by-house surveillance grid disguised as sanitation. The stated goal -- cheaper code enforcement -- is plausible and even popular. The unresolved question is whether a city should hold a continuously updated AI score for every home in town, with the power to mail notices and issue citations, before any legislature, court, or homeowner consented to it. Dallas's October vote will be the first real test of where that line sits.

Peter,
**New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District is a critical open seat.** Holding it will be essential to building the U.S. House majority that Democrats need to stand up to this administration and fight for families everywhere.
That's why we've endorsed **Stefany Shaheen** , Peter.
Stefany's life changed when her eldest daughter, Elle, was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at eight years old and nearly lost her life. For more than 15 years since, Stefany has fought to secure insurance coverage for conditions like Elle's, advance groundbreaking medical research, improve treatments, and accelerate the development of cures.
Stefany is running for Congress because Donald Trump and congressional Republicans are undermining medical research and cutting Medicaid and healthcare for children, seniors, and veterans, all while delivering tax breaks to billionaires and corporations. She knew it was not enough to just be outraged; that New Hampshire needs leaders prepared to step up and fight back.
Stefany brings experience in business, public service, and advocacy to this race. She has spent her career confronting difficult challenges and refusing to give up on the people who need her. This is exactly the kind of leadership the Granite State deserves in Congress.

*By subscribing to my e-mail updates, you are authorizing me to send regular e-mail updates from my office to your e-mail account.
#
# **The Right to Vote is Under Attack**
_It's Time to Fight Back_
The message is simple. We cannot sit on the sidelines as our right and access to voting is under attack. We must vote in record numbers to show that the power remains with the people.

**What Experts Have to Say**
[Senator Hughes recently held a telephone townhall](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18363) about attacks on voting rights to help constituents understand what's happening with voting rights and mail in ballots. He and his guests also discussed what people need to know about voting in the [next election on November 3rd](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18364).

[**LISTEN TO THE TELEPHONE TOWNHALL FROM AUGUST 24TH ON OUR WEBSITE.**](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18363)
[](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18365)

_Senator Hughes was joined by expert guests including: _
* [Barbara R. Arnwine](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18366), President and Founder, [Transformative Justice Coalition](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18367)
* [Commissioner Jamila Winder](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18352), Chair of the [Montgomery County Board of Commissioners](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18354)
* [Commissioner Omar Sabir](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18355), Chair of the [Philadelphia City Commissioners](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18356)

_**Key Takeaways from the Conversation**_
* **VOTING BY MAIL IS STILL LEGAL._You can still vote by mail in Pennsylvania in the November election._ If you are feeling confused about news or information you're reading, reach out to your local county voting or commissioner's office for the latest and most accurate information on mail in voting.**

* **The Trump Administration does not have authority to oversee elections. The constitution makes it clear that states are required and authorized to run their own elections. Congress does have authority to "make or alter" state regulations concerning congressional elections, but the President does not have that authority by himself.**

* **Do not be discouraged! In Pennsylvania, leaders, advocates, and election officials, both Democrat and Republican, are committed to keeping Pennsylvania elections fair, safe, and secure.**

* * *
**Make a Plan to Vote**
**_Important Dates_**
* Register to vote by: Oct. 19, 2026
* Request a mail-in or absentee ballot by: Oct. 27, 2026
* Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026. Polls will be open from 7AM to 8PM

**_Voting Resources_**
To register to vote, apply for a mail in ballot, or learn more about polling places, connect with your county commissioner's office.

**Philadelphia County Commissioners**
* 215-686-3469
* [vote.phila.gov](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18357)

Philadelphia has 10 satellite election offices in each of the city's 10 council districts. Location and service information is listed online at [vote.phila.gov](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18356).

**Montgomery County Voter Services**
* 610-278-3000
* [www.montgomerycountypa.gov/departments/voter-services](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172456.172236.69&gen=1&mailing_linkid=18358)

Montgomery County has a mobile satellite office van that visits different parts of the county to bring voting services like voter registration and mail-in ballot applications to the people. Five women. One moment to make history.
Five women. One moment to make history.

| | Peter, Something is happening this November that has never happened in American history: Three Indigenous women are running for top statewide offices in the same year. And a fourth is defending the seat where she made history in 2018. **Mary Peltola** , a Yup’ik leader and the first Alaska Native ever elected to Congress, is challenging Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and just outpolled him in Alaska’s primary. **Peggy Flanagan** , a citizen of the White Earth Nation, won her primary by roughly 20 points. If she wins in November, she’ll be the first Native American woman ever to serve in the U.S. Senate. **Deb Haaland** , a citizen of Laguna Pueblo and the first Native American Cabinet secretary, won her primary with more than 70% of the vote. She would be the first Native American woman ever elected governor. **Sharice Davids** , a citizen of the Ho-Chunk Nation and one of the first two Native American women ever elected to Congress, is defending her Kansas seat after winning her primary with 83%. **Claire Valdez,** a citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation and a union organizer serving in the New York State Assembly, won her primary in New York’s 7th District this June — and is now poised to grow Indigenous representation in Congress. Here’s the thing: all five are tied or ahead in their races. But leading a poll isn’t even remotely the same as winning on Election Day. The final stretch is the expensive part, and that’s why Indigenous Women Lead PAC exists — to close the funding gaps and make sure these women cross the finish line. clean_body: Five women. One moment to make history. Five women. One moment to make history. | ~~ | | Peter, Something is happening this November that has never happened in American history: Three Indigenous women are running for top statewide offices in the same year. And a fourth is defending the seat where she made history in 2018. Mary Peltola , a Yup’ik leader and the first Alaska Native ever elected to Congress, is challenging Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and just outpolled him in Alaska’s primary. Peggy Flanagan , a citizen of the White Earth Nation, won her primary by roughly 20 points. If she wins in November, she’ll be the first Native American woman ever to serve in the U.S. Senate. Deb Haaland , a citizen of Laguna Pueblo and the first Native American Cabinet secretary, won her primary with more than 70% of the vote. She would be the first Native American woman ever elected governor. Sharice Davids , a citizen of the Ho-Chunk Nation and one of the first two Native American women ever elected to Congress, is defending her Kansas seat after winning her primary with 83%. Claire Valdez, a citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation and a union organizer serving in the New York State Assembly, won her primary in New York’s 7th District this June — and is now poised to grow Indigenous representation in Congress. Here’s the thing: all five are tied or ahead in their races. But leading a poll isn’t even remotely the same as winning on Election Day. The final stretch is the expensive part, and that’s why Indigenous Women Lead PAC exists — to close the funding gaps and make sure these women cross the finish line. clean_body: Let’s clear the air.| | | | | - Peter , I flew above battlefields, passing burning husks of armored vehicles, and in Iraq I poured enough sand out of my boots to fill a desert. You would think that after flying an Apache helicopter through an active war zone, and having God knows how many stray bullets shot my direction, there’s not a thing on this planet that could scare me. I thought so too, until my team reminded me about what’s coming in the next few days. Let me explain. This campaign’s bigger than anything I’ve done in Iraq. Rather than covering for a team on the ground, the fate of more than 10 million people will be decided in November. Campaigning isn’t easy, and sometimes it feels like the weight of the world is on my shoulders. Just before I typed this email, my team reminded me about our upcoming End-of-Quarter fundraising deadline. This isn’t just an arbitrary deadline; this is one of our last BIG goals before the November election. I’m not going to ask you to dig deep into your pockets. All I’m asking is a $1 or more donation, which will go right into my campaign's war chest and help me and President Trump take down the Democrat machine come November. As a combat veteran and a patriot - I give you my word that every dollar matters, and I’m eternally thankful for ANY gift you can make. Time is running out. Thank you for listening, and I hope I can count on your help. | | — John James Republican Nominee for Governor | | Paid for by John James for MI | | 35744 Van Dyke Avenue, Sterling Heights, MI 48312 The use of John James' military images, uniforms, or personnel does not imply endorsement by the Department of War or any branch of the U.S. military. |

clean_body: | | | | Good evening, Peter. It’s Cait Conley. It is an honor to know that there are so many people out there who believe in our campaign. And I do not take your support lightly. I know how much every dollar matters – I come from a working-class family where we made ends meet, followed by a career in public service and sacrifice. I joined the Army after 9/11. I deployed six times overseas, serving in combat zones like Iraq and Afghanistan, hunting down brutal terrorists to keep America and the world safe. So I promise, we are putting your contributions to work building the most competitive operation possible. I want you to hear this: Mike Lawler is beatable. But it isn’t going to be easy. The richest man in the world and the President of the United States have both decided that I am a threat, and are spending an absurd amount of money to stop me. Trump is spending more money here than he is on any other House race nationwide. So we are sprinting at this fight, head on. My opponent has billionaires backing him. | | | | | | | | | | | | Hi Peter,
Time is ticking, and we need **YOU NOW! 🚨**
There are **ONLY 16 DAYS** until ballots drop and voters begin deciding the future of our community. Every door we knock on and every conversation we have directly shapes the outcome of this election.
Let’s hit the streets and show everyone what _La Máquina_ is made of! Bring a friend, bring your energy, and come build power with us. At _La Máquina_ , we value our community and our volunteers, and yes, delicious _pan dulce_ will be waiting for you bright and early! 🥐☕
Join us for our[**Educators for Adelita Canvass**](https://us.list-manage.com/11wxMFb57MX?e=f7c3700ccb&c2id=444a9f520cb2092400304c5b9d69cefc)**** this Saturday, September 26th at 8:30AM from our **Tucson HQ at 2720 East Broadway BLVD**.**OR** Let’s go to Bisbee this Saturday, September 26th at 8:30AM for our [**Bisbee: All in for Adelita canvass**](https://us.list-manage.com/vY6qr4qSxwX?e=f7c3700ccb&c2id=444a9f520cb2092400304c5b9d69cefc) , leaving from our Tucson HQ **2720 East Broadway BLVD** at **7:00AM SHARP!**
Let’s fight for our people, our pueblo, especially our future, it is on the line!

clean_body: Peter, I'm going to make a prediction... When the votes are counted this November, the radical left is going to be in a state of total shock. And the political establishment is going to spend weeks trying to explain what hit them. But that only happens if Republicans like you are on record before the Midterms. That is how consequential this moment is. But here is the part the pundits won't tell you. None of that happens automatically. The Democrats are at war with the American people -- open borders, defunding ICE, eliminating voter ID, putting men in women's sports. You name it, they are on the wrong side of it. And yet they are running the most radical, well-funded Senate candidates in states across this country who are counting on Republicans to stay home and let them walk right in. I will not let that happen. And I don't think you will either. I made you a prediction at the beginning of this email. I stand by every word of it. But that prediction is built on one assumption -- that Republicans like you are engaged and ready to fight. That is where your assessment comes in. Sincerely, Newt Gingrich Former Speaker of the House | Paid for by the NRSC. Not authorized by any candidate or candidate's committee. |

Fellow Conservative: As we race toward the midterm elections, there are two things Americans must know. **1) U.S. Senate races are _NATIONAL_ elections that impact ALL AMERICANS regardless of where you live.** **2) Electing strong _CONSERVATIVES_ is what matters, because another spineless Republican majority will not save our country.** Let's break these down... First, we often hear people say they don't really care about elections outside their home state. They can't vote for the candidates, so why bother? The reason is simple: _U.S. Senators make national policies that impact the lives of ALL Americans._ So while you may not be able to vote for them, their votes in Washington affect you and your family. **This is why conservatives in all 50 states must use their Constitutionally protected freedom of speech to influence the outcomes of Senate races around the country.** But if the entire Senate map is important to every American, which candidates matter most? The answer: _Conservatives_. Notice that it's not Republicans because many Republicans will not fight for our priorities when it matters. We've all painfully watched the current Senate Republican majority squander its mandate and fail to pass even the most popular policies like voter ID. Meanwhile, it has worked with the Democrats to spend so much that our national debt now exceeds $40 trillion. **The bottom line is that electing more moderate, pro-establishment Republicans is not worth our time and money.** That's why the Senate Conservatives Fund has selected eight conservative candidates across the nation who deserve our votes _AND_ our financial support.
